sub: How a shallow placenta causes preeclampsia, why placental hormones unmask diabetes, and how to tell apart the causes of late bleeding.

pretest.q: Which placental change starts the chain of events in preeclampsia?
o: Shallow remodeling of the spiral arteries
Placental attachment over the internal os
pretest.why: In preeclampsia, cytotrophoblast fails to convert the maternal spiral arteries into wide channels. The placenta becomes ischemic and releases sFlt-1, which injures the mother's endothelium.

w.Premature separation of the placenta: That is placental abruption, a painful bleeding emergency that preeclampsia can trigger. It is a complication, not the starting defect of the disease.
w.Placental attachment over the internal o: That describes placenta previa, which bleeds painlessly from the lower segment. It has no link to the vascular defect behind preeclampsia.
w.Villi invading through the myometrium: That is the accreta spectrum, caused by missing decidua over a scar. There trophoblast invades too deeply, the opposite of preeclampsia.

pretest.q: Which hormone chiefly causes insulin resistance in the second half of pregnancy?
pretest.why: Human placental lactogen rises with placental mass and blunts insulin action, so the mother burns fat and saves glucose for the fetus. When her beta cells cannot keep up, gestational diabetes appears.

w.Human chorionic gonadotropin: hCG peaks near 10 weeks and rescues the corpus luteum. It is falling just as insulin resistance starts to climb in the second half of pregnancy.
w.Relaxin: Relaxin loosens pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix. It has no meaningful effect on how muscle and fat respond to insulin.
w.Oxytocin: Oxytocin contracts the uterus in labor and the breast myoepithelial cells during nursing. It does not oppose insulin in its target tissues.

pretest.q: An Rh-negative woman with a negative antibody screen is at 28 weeks. Which step best protects a future Rh-positive baby?
pretest.why: Anti-D immune globulin at 28 weeks, and again within 72 hours of delivering an Rh-positive baby, clears fetal red cells before she makes her own IgG anti-D. It prevents sensitization but cannot reverse it once antibodies exist.

w.Antenatal betamethasone: Betamethasone matures fetal lungs when preterm delivery is expected. It does nothing to maternal antibody formation against fetal red cells.
w.Low-dose aspirin: Aspirin lowers preeclampsia risk in high-risk patients by improving placental blood flow. It does not prevent Rh sensitization.
w.Intrauterine transfusion: Transfusion treats a fetus already made anemic by maternal antibodies. She has none yet, so there is nothing to treat and no sensitization to prevent.

body: How does blood pressure change, and when is it preeclampsia?

Blood pressure normally falls early in pregnancy. Progesterone and nitric oxide relax the arterioles, and the placenta adds a low-resistance circuit. So **systemic vascular resistance** drops even though blood volume and cardiac output rise. Pressure bottoms out in the second trimester and returns toward the pre-pregnancy baseline by term. A reading of 140/90 or higher on two occasions is therefore abnormal at any stage. **Preeclampsia** is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria of 300 mg or more per 24 hours, or with end-organ damage. The table below sorts it from its neighbors.
New hypertension; no proteinuria or organ damage
New hypertension plus proteinuria (ratio 0.3 or more); normal labs
160/110 or higher, platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 mg/dL, transaminases twice normal, pulmonary edema, new headache or visual change
Hemolysis (schistocytes, high LDH), AST or ALT twice normal, platelets under 100,000
What does preeclampsia look like, and what do HELLP and eclampsia add?

Many patients feel well, so the disease is found by checking blood pressure and urine protein at every prenatal visit. The warning symptoms come from organ injury. A persistent **headache** and visual changes come from cerebral vasoconstriction and edema. Pain in the **right upper quadrant** or epigastrium, often with nausea, means the swollen liver capsule is stretching. Sudden facial and hand swelling, brisk reflexes with clonus and rapid weight gain suggest severe disease, but mild leg swelling alone is common and proves nothing. Labs look for organ injury: urine protein, platelets, creatinine and liver enzymes.

HELLP is a microangiopathy. Damaged endothelium shreds red cells into schistocytes, which causes hemolysis with high LDH and low haptoglobin. Fibrin in the liver sinusoids raises AST and ALT, and platelets are used up. Bleeding under the liver capsule can form a subcapsular hematoma that may rupture, and DIC can follow. Blood pressure may be only mildly raised, so epigastric pain, nausea and low platelets need these labs even when pressure is normal. **Eclampsia** is a generalized tonic-clonic seizure from cerebral vasospasm and edema. It can follow mild hypertension and can strike before delivery, during labor or after birth; postpartum seizures usually come within 48 hours of delivery. A seizure in a pregnant or recently delivered woman is eclampsia until proven otherwise.
Why does a shallow placenta injure the mother's endothelium?

In a normal pregnancy, cytotrophoblast invades the decidua and inner myometrium and replaces the muscular wall of the maternal **spiral arteries**. This turns them into wide channels that cannot constrict. In preeclampsia that remodeling stays shallow, so the arteries keep their muscle, flow falls and the placenta becomes ischemic. The ischemic placenta releases {{rp27_sflt|sFlt-1}}, a soluble decoy receptor that traps VEGF and placental growth factor. Without free VEGF, **endothelial dysfunction** spreads through the mother. Arterioles constrict, capillaries leak, swollen glomerular endothelium lets protein through, and platelets activate. The placental vessels show fibrinoid necrosis. Because the placenta is the source, **delivery** is the only cure.

Risk factors follow from the mechanism, because more placenta or a poorer vascular bed raises the risk. They include prior preeclampsia, nulliparity, multifetal gestation such as twins, chronic hypertension, pregestational diabetes, chronic kidney disease, antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus, and obesity. A molar pregnancy can cause preeclampsia before 20 weeks, the one exception to the timing rule. High-risk patients take **low-dose aspirin** (81 mg), started at about 12 weeks and continued until delivery, which lowers their risk.
How is severe preeclampsia treated, and why magnesium?

A pressure of 160/110 or higher risks maternal stroke, so it is lowered quickly with IV **labetalol**, IV hydralazine or oral nifedipine. Hydralazine dilates arterioles directly and can cause reflex tachycardia and, with long use, drug-induced lupus. Labetalol is avoided in asthma. Methyldopa, a central alpha-2 agonist, is an older choice for chronic hypertension in pregnancy and can cause a Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia. ACE inhibitors are avoided in pregnancy because they injure the fetal kidney.

**Magnesium sulfate** is the drug of choice to prevent seizures, and it also treats eclamptic seizures. It does not lower blood pressure. It continues through labor and for 24 hours after delivery, because eclampsia can strike postpartum.

Delivery removes the source of sFlt-1 and is the definitive treatment. The sicker the mother, or the closer to term, the sooner she delivers. Far from term, a stable patient may be watched in the hospital while betamethasone matures the fetal lungs.

Magnesium is cleared only by the kidneys, so toxicity is most likely when preeclampsia has cut urine output. The **patellar reflex**, respiratory rate and urine output are checked often. Loss of deep tendon reflexes comes first, then respiratory depression, then cardiac arrest. The antidote is IV **calcium gluconate**, which opposes magnesium at the nerve and muscle membrane.
Why do placental hormones unmask diabetes, and what does that do to the fetus?

As the placenta grows, it secretes more and more {{rp27_hpl|human placental lactogen}}. With cortisol and progesterone, it causes **insulin resistance** in the second half of pregnancy. Lactogen also breaks down fat, so between meals the mother runs on **free fatty acids** and ketones and saves glucose and amino acids for the fetus. This keeps the fetal glucose supply steady even when she fasts. A woman whose beta cells cannot raise insulin output enough develops **gestational diabetes**.

Risk factors are obesity, prior gestational diabetes, a prior macrosomic baby, **polycystic** ovary syndrome, a family history of type 2 diabetes and older age. High-risk women are tested at the first prenatal visit, and everyone else at 24 to 28 weeks, when insulin resistance peaks. The two-step method is a nonfasting 1-hour 50-g **glucose challenge** followed, if abnormal, by a fasting 3-hour 100-g test. The one-step method is a single fasting 2-hour 75-g test. Diet and exercise come first, and insulin is added if glucose stays high. Treatment lowers macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and preeclampsia.

The fetal effects follow one rule: glucose crosses the placenta, but maternal insulin does not. The fetus answers hyperglycemia with beta-cell **hyperplasia** and hyperinsulinemia. Insulin is a fetal growth hormone, so fat builds up into **macrosomia**, which sets up shoulder dystocia. At birth the glucose supply stops but the extra insulin does not, causing neonatal hypoglycemia. Insulin also delays **surfactant** production, so respiratory distress is more likely. High fetal oxygen use drives polycythemia, and hypocalcemia can follow. Fetal polyuria causes polyhydramnios. The mother has more preeclampsia and cesarean delivery. Her resistance vanishes after delivery, but her lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes stays high, so she is retested after birth.
Pregestational diabetes harms earlier and differently

Gestational diabetes begins after organogenesis, so it causes overgrowth, not malformations. Pregestational diabetes exposes the embryo to high glucose during weeks 3 to 8, which raises the risk of congenital anomalies. These include heart defects such as **transposition** of the great arteries and VSD, neural tube defects and **caudal regression** syndrome, along with stillbirth. Glucose must be tightly controlled before conception.
Which placental problem is bleeding in the third trimester?

Late bleeding is sorted by pain and by where the placenta sits. In **placenta previa**, the placenta lies over or near the internal os. As the lower segment stretches, it bleeds bright red and painlessly, and the uterus stays soft. A digital exam could tear the placenta, so ultrasound comes first, and delivery is by cesarean. In {{rp27_abruption|abruption}}, a normally implanted placenta separates early from the uterine wall and bleeds into the gap behind it. The uterus is painful, tender and hypertonic. A concealed retroplacental clot can cause shock and fetal distress out of proportion to the blood seen. Hypertension, cocaine, smoking and trauma raise the risk, and consumed clotting factors can cause DIC.

Two more problems hide in the attachment. The {{rp27_accreta|placenta accreta spectrum}} forms where the **decidua basalis** is missing, usually over a cesarean scar. Villi then attach to the myometrium (accreta), invade it (increta) or pass through it, sometimes into the bladder (percreta). It is painless before delivery but bleeds massively when the placenta will not separate. In **vasa previa**, unprotected fetal vessels cross the os inside the membranes. When the membranes rupture, the vessels tear, and the blood lost is the fetus's, so fetal bradycardia appears while the mother stays stable. Ultrasound can find all three of these placental problems before labor.
The differential also includes **uterine rupture**, usually through a prior cesarean scar. It causes sudden pain, a retreating presenting part and fetal bradycardia, often with little vaginal blood.
Why can a placental abruption cause disseminated intravascular coagulation?

The decidua and placenta are among the richest sources of tissue factor in the body. When the placenta shears off, tissue factor from the damaged decidua enters the maternal circulation and triggers the extrinsic pathway. The large retroplacental clot also consumes fibrinogen and platelets. Fibrin forms in small vessels while the remaining blood loses its ability to clot, so bleeding from the placental bed, IV sites and wounds worsens. A falling fibrinogen is the earliest warning, and delivery plus blood products stops the process.
How does an Rh-negative mother come to attack her next baby?

An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus meets fetal red cells through **fetomaternal hemorrhage**. This happens mostly at delivery, but also with miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, abruption, trauma or amniocentesis. This exposure triggers **sensitization**. Her first response is IgM, which cannot cross the placenta, so the first pregnancy is spared. In the next Rh-positive pregnancy, memory cells make IgG anti-D, which crosses the placenta and coats fetal red cells so the spleen destroys them. This {{rp27_alloimm|alloimmunization}} causes hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

The fetus becomes anemic and, when severe, develops **hydrops**, meaning edema, ascites and effusions from high-output heart failure. After birth the placenta no longer clears bilirubin, so unconjugated bilirubin can enter the basal ganglia and cause kernicterus. Prevention is passive. **Anti-D immune globulin** is given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivering an Rh-positive baby or of a bleeding event at 12 weeks or later. It clears fetal cells before the mother responds, and a {{rp27_kb|Kleihauer-Betke test}} sizes the dose. Once she is sensitized, immune globulin cannot help, and the fetal anemia needs intrauterine transfusion. ABO disease is different. A type O mother already has IgG anti-A and anti-B, so even her first pregnancy can be affected. Even so, the disease is mild: jaundice appears in the first day of life and phototherapy usually treats it, the Coombs test is only weakly positive, and it cannot be prevented.
How are preterm labor and ruptured membranes managed?

Preterm labor means contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks, and the goal is to buy time. Risk factors are prior preterm birth, multifetal gestation, a short cervix, infection and smoking, and vaginal progesterone lowers the risk when the cervix is short. A **tocolytic** such as nifedipine, indomethacin or terbutaline delays delivery by about 48 hours. That is long enough for **betamethasone** to mature the fetal lungs. Indomethacin is used only before 32 weeks, because it can close the ductus arteriosus and cause oligohydramnios. Magnesium before 32 weeks gives fetal **neuroprotection** against cerebral palsy, and group B strep prophylaxis starts when her status is unknown.

Premature rupture of membranes is leakage of fluid before labor. Pooling in the vagina, alkaline fluid that turns nitrazine paper blue, and a fern pattern when the fluid dries confirm it. It invites ascending infection. Chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection) shows as maternal fever with fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness or foul-smelling fluid. It is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and delivery, and it raises the risk of neonatal sepsis.
How is fetal growth checked, and what restricts it?

From 20 to 36 weeks, fundal height in centimeters roughly equals gestational age in weeks, so a gap of more than 3 cm prompts ultrasound. Ultrasound uses the head, abdomen and femur measurements to calculate the **estimated fetal weight**, and fetal growth restriction means an estimate under the 10th percentile.

**Symmetric** restriction starts early, from aneuploidy or congenital infection, and shrinks the head and body alike. **Asymmetric**, head-sparing restriction starts late, from placental insufficiency as in preeclampsia, hypertension or smoking. The fetus diverts blood to its brain, so the abdomen lags, and poor kidney perfusion causes oligohydramnios. These infants face stillbirth and asphyxia, and as adults more hypertension, type 2 diabetes and **metabolic syndrome**, because poor fetal nutrition programs later metabolism. Macrosomia is the opposite error, usually from maternal diabetes.
Which late itches and liver diseases matter, and what is amniotic fluid embolism?

Late itching is sorted by the rash and by what it means for the fetus. The table also lists acute fatty liver of pregnancy and **amniotic fluid embolism**, a sudden labor emergency in which amniotic fluid enters the maternal circulation.
Itchy palms and soles, no rash, high bile acids
Bile acids reach the fetus: stillbirth risk; ursodiol, delivery near term
Papules in abdominal striae, sparing the umbilicus
Periumbilical blisters from IgG against a skin anchoring protein
IgG crosses the placenta: newborn blisters, growth restriction
Liver failure with hypoglycemia; microvesicular fat in hepatocytes, sometimes from a fetal fatty acid oxidation defect (LCHAD deficiency)
Sudden hypoxemia, hypotension and DIC in labor

body.q: A woman at 34 weeks has new hypertension and proteinuria. Which reasoning explains why delivery, not drugs, cures her?
o: Lowering blood pressure removes the stimulus for proteinuria, so drugs alone reverse the disease
The ischemic placenta keeps releasing sFlt-1, so only removing it ends the endothelial injury
Delivery shrinks the plasma volume, and volume overload is what raises her pressure
Magnesium cures the disease, and delivery only lets the magnesium be stopped
body.why: Preeclampsia is driven by the placenta. Shallow spiral artery remodeling leaves it ischemic, and it secretes sFlt-1, which injures maternal endothelium. Antihypertensives prevent stroke but leave that source untouched, so proteinuria, low platelets and liver injury can progress while the pressure looks controlled. Magnesium only prevents seizures. Once the placenta is delivered, sFlt-1 falls and the disease resolves over days.

grid.q: Which of these are severe features of preeclampsia?
items: New headache that does not respond to medication
Liver enzymes twice the upper limit of normal
